SIMLAB food tests and red-cabbage indicator

Use separate fresh aliquots for Benedict, iodine, Biuret and lipid testing.
The added food stocks are ideal reference materials, not branded foods.
Glucose, fructose, maltose and lactose are reducing-sugar references;
sucrose is the non-reducing reference. Starch and albumin are standardized
mass-concentration reference preparations; vegetable oil is a model mixture.
Benedict and Biuret are premixed formulations, so one molarity does not
describe the complete reagent. Sugar stock molarity remains user-editable.

Benedict: an interpretable result requires heating an alkaline mixture.
Reducing activity produces Cu2O solid; residual Cu(II) can remain blue.
The green/yellow/orange/brick-red teaching scale uses a nominal 0.07 mol/L
Cu(II) reagent and reducing equivalents. It is not a validated calibration,
limit-of-detection model, or proof that a particular sugar is present.
Fructose responds through alkaline isomerisation. Non-sugar reducing agents
can also interfere in real food extracts.

Non-reducing sugar: compare negative untreated sucrose with a positive
fresh hydrolysate. The model requires acid plus heating, cooling and
neutralisation BEFORE Benedict is added, then a second heating step.
A negative untreated result alone does not identify a non-reducing sugar.
Hydrolysis is treated as complete after the designated virtual treatment;
no rate law, catalytic acid dependence, side degradation or quantitative
hydrolysis yield is claimed. The hydrolyzed state travels with aliquots.

Water bath: warming to 90 C and a 180-second hot hold at >=80 C run on an
accelerated teaching clock. The standard apparatus heater also supports
this accelerated hold. These are simulator settings, not a universal lab
method or a prediction of actual reaction time. Cool samples before
neutralisation and interpretation. Organic solvent samples are excluded.

Biuret: a violet Cu(II)-peptide complex indicates peptide groups in the
albumin reference. Blue is the negative reference. No solid or gas is formed.
The premixed reagent supplies alkaline conditions. No heating is required.

Iodine: blue-black starch/polyiodide inclusion colour; it is not a solid
precipitate. The colour may weaken on heating and should be read after
cooling. A yellow-brown result is negative for starch in these reference
samples, not proof that no carbohydrate is present.

Lipid emulsion: first prepare the oil/ethanol extract; then transfer it
into water. White cloudiness is a physical dispersion of lipid droplets,
not a precipitate or a chemical reaction. Water/ethanol alone stays clear.
An oil layer or pre-existing cloudiness is not the developed test endpoint.
Extraction efficiency, phase volume, droplet size and emulsion stability
are not calculated quantitatively.

Anthocyanins: red-cabbage pigments change forms with pH. The displayed
colour anchors run red/pink in acid, purple/violet near neutral, then blue,
green and yellow at increasing alkalinity. Shades are approximate and
depend on extraction, pigment concentration, temperature, age and time.
Strong-alkali degradation and photobleaching are not simulated. Reference
buffers have assigned pH; their capacity is not computed. Simple acid/base
mixtures use ideal 25 C charge balance, including weak acid/base and
carbonate equilibria; CO2 loss and activity coefficients are ignored.
Food matrices with uncharacterized buffering do not receive an invented pH.

Sources
AQA GCSE Biology Practical Handbook: food tests, interpretation and controls:
https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/biology/AQA-8461-PRACTICALS-HB.PDF

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology sample lab book: food tests,
including Biuret, iodine and sequential ethanol-emulsion procedure:
https://www.pearson.com/content/dam/one-dot-com/one-dot-com/international-schools/pdfs/secondary-curriculum/international-gcse/science/IGBiologyLabBooksample.pdf

Ministry of Education, Saint Lucia: Biology Students Manual, experiment 12,
non-reducing sugar test (hydrolysis, neutralisation, then Benedict):
https://camdu.edu.lc/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Biology-Students-Manual-Part-2-of-4.pdf

CLEAPSS GL018 Food tests: coverage of established food-test methods:
https://science.cleapss.org.uk/Resource-Info/GL018-Food-tests.aspx

American Chemical Society: Red Cabbage Indicator:
https://www.acs.org/education/activities/red-cabbage-indicator.html

Royal Society of Chemistry: Rainbow Cabbage (approximate colour scale):
https://edu.rsc.org/download?ac=512305

All equations, colour renderings and inferences are educational models;
they are not experimental measurements or confirmatory analysis of a real food.
